Notes: Gross Examination: The submission consisted of three 5 x 2 x 2 mm to 10 x 6 x 3 mm samples of popliteal lymph node. Histopathology: In sections reviewed, the samples consist of sheets of well-differentiated adipocytes and connective tissue. There are scant interstitial macrophages or lymphocytes. Lymph node is not identified. Diagnosis: Open. Comment: Chelsea, unfortunately it appears that these samples are not representative of the lymph node. Generally speaking, I recommend removal of an entire node for histopathology; the diagnosis of lymphoma often depends on nodal architecture (absent or disoriented in incisional biopsies), and lymphoid tissue is easy to artefactually distort during the biopsy process, leading to non-diagnostic samples with cells that cannot be interpreted. If you choose to resample this node I would be happy to examine a resubmission for a reduced fee.

GROSS EXAMINATION: RHS Lip mass - 5 x 5 x 6 mm tissue HISTOPATHOLOGY: The tissue is composed of epidermis and dermis. The epidermis is partially ulcerated. Within the epidermis and dermis there are sheets of neoplastic round to polygonal cells with moderate to abundant about amount of clear cytoplasm, moderate to marked anisokaryosis with multiple prominent nucleoli and 20 mitotic figures per approximately 2.37 mm, 10, 400x hpf equivalent. The neoplastic cells extend to one of the lateral margins of the tissue examined. The cells are surrounded by moderate numbers of lymphocytes and plasma cells, and in 1 area neutrophils and multinucleate macrophages. DIAGNOSIS: RHS Lip mass - Anaplastic Neoplasm with ulceration COMMENTS: The neoplastic cells extend to one of the lateral margins of the tissue examined. Dr Geoff Orbell and Dr Bernie Vaatstra have also looked at the tissue. DDX Amelanotic Melanoma, vs anaplastic round cell tumour (epitheliotropic lymphoma), vs poorly differentiated Carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry may be useful to differentiate - but often anaplastic cell have lost their markers. In this site, and is there are no other oral or skin lesions then Amelanotic Melanoma would be our first consideration. Malignant Melanomas often recur at the site, as they are locally invasive to soft tissue and bone. These neoplasms metastasise via lymphatics and blood vessels to regional lymph nodes and lungs, and then to brain, heart, kidney, liver and spleen. Lung metastasis is often slow to grow. Oral malignant melanomas have a worse prognosis than cutaneous melanomas. Oral melanomas, with invasion, >/= 4 mitotic figures per 10 hpf (400x) and >/= 30% nuclear atypia, have a worse prognosis. Ref: Prognostic Markers for Canine Melanocytic Neoplasms: A Comparative Review of the Literature and Goals for Future Investigation Vet Pathol January 2011 48: 54-72, Smedley et al. REVIEW ARTICLE A Comparative Review of Melanocytic Neoplasms, S. H. SMITH, M. H. GOLDSCHMIDT, AND P. M. MCMANUS. Vet Pathol 39:651-678 (2002) Most oral melanomas have a worse prognosis than cutaneous melanomas, as most are aggressive and recurrence or metastasis is expected in 60 to 80%. Oral and Dermal lesions that are pedunculated generally behave benignly, either because of their biology and / or ease of complete removal. Benign (low malignant potential) oral melanomas are small <2cm, well to heavily pigmented, and have a median survival time of approximately 3 years. 5% died of melanoma. Oral Melanomas with <4 mitotic figures per 10 hpf (400x) and <30% nuclear atypia have a favourable prognosis. Oral Melanomas with >4 mitotic figures per 10 hpf (400x) and >30% nuclear atypia have a poor prognosis. Refs: Tumors in Domestic Animals Fifth Edition. Edited by Donald J. Meuten. 2017 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. History: Noticed enlarged mandibular LN, 2 weeks ago. Bilaterally severely enlarged mandibular LNs. Prescapular LNs, inguinal LNs, popliteal LNs. Sampled R prescap, L popliteal, R popliteal. Slides examined: 10/10 (4x scap, 3x L pop, 3x R pop) Cytology description: A total of ten slides have been examined and are cytologically similar. The slides are of large numbers of lymphoid cells in a background of variable amounts of blood. The lymphoid cells are predominantly composed of intermediate to large lymphocytes, characterized by round to oval nucleus containing dispersed chromatin with single to multiple somewhat large nucleoli and mildly increased amounts of basophilic cytoplasm. Infrequent small lymphocytes are seen. There are low numbers of macrophages and neutrophils. Interpretation: Lymphoma Comment: The lymphoid cells from all the sites are homogeneous with predominance of intermediate to large lymphocytes, most consistent with a lymphoma. Canine lymphoma is often multicentric with involvement of multiple lymph nodes and sometimes internal organs, such as the liver and spleen. Additional staging diagnostics may include a complete blood count, serum biochemistries, urinalysis, and abdominal and thoracic imaging. You may also consider immunophenotyping (immunocytochemistry) to determine whether this lymphoma is of B cell or T cell origin, as this may offer additional prognostic information. If you would like to proceed with this step, please let us know. These submitted cytology slides can be used for this test (immunocytochemistry).

GROSS EXAMINATION: Left Chest - 25 x 20 x 10 mm tissue Inguinal region - 10 x 4 x 4 mm punch of tissue HISTOPATHOLOGY: Left Chest - The tissue is composed of a lymph node and surrounding adipose tissue. Approximately two thirds of the lymph node has been replaced by densely cellular sheets of neoplastic lymphocytes with greater than 5 mitotic figures per high-power field (400 X). The neoplastic lymphocytes are intermediate sized (2 times the size of red blood cells), with a scant amount of cytoplasm and moderate anisokaryosis. Inguinal region - The tissue is composed of a section of lymph node and adjacent adipose tissue and connective tissue. The lymph node tissue has been replaced by densely cellular sheets of neoplastic lymphocytes with greater than 5 mitotic figures per high-power field (400 X). The neoplastic lymphocytes are intermediate sized (2 times the size of red blood cells), with a scant amount of cytoplasm and moderate anisokaryosis. Adjacent to this there are large areas of coagulative necrosis admixed with peripheral small numbers of neutrophils and areas of granulation tissue proliferation (fibroblasts and small blood vessels). DIAGNOSIS: Left Chest - Lymphoma Inguinal region - Lymphoma with necrosis COMMENTS: Canine Lymphoma is often multicentric with involvement of multiple lymph nodes and internal organs such as the liver, spleen and bone marrow. Immunohistochemistry can be performed to differentiate B and T cell Lymphoma, which have a slightly different prognosis, but at the moment we only have T cell markers available. Diffuse nodal lymphomas are the most common form of lymphoma in animals. In dogs B cell Lymphomas account for 60 to 80% of all lymphomas, and diffuse large B cell Lymphoma is the most common, is high grade and can be treated with aggressive chemotherapy. Dogs with B-cell lymphoma may be more likely to achieve complete remission, have longer remission duration and survival remission, than dogs with T-cell lymphoma. Ref: Dr William Vernau. Lymphoma in Animals: Application of the WHO Lymphoma Classification Scheme and useful adjunctive diagnostics. NZ Path Society annual meeting 2014.

GROSS EXAMINATION: SQ mass R side mid-Back - 7 tissues ranging from 2 x 3 x 6 mm to 3 x 10 x 19 mm, from a 9 x 10 cm SQ mass HISTOPATHOLOGY: Some of the tissues are composed of adipose tissue infiltrated by densely cellular sheets of neoplastic lymphocytes with 2 mitotic figures per high-power field (400 X) and many individually necrotic cells. The cells have a scant amount of cytoplasm and are small to intermediate sized with moderate anisokaryosis and prominent nucleoli. Multifocally there are areas of necrosis. Some of the tissues are composed of epidermis, dermis, pannicular skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. Other tissues are composed of adipose tissue only. DIAGNOSIS: SQ mass R side mid-Back - Lymphoma with necrosis COMMENTS: Cutaneous Lymphoma can be T cell (usually epitheliotropic) or B cell (usually nonepitheliotropic) but immunohistochemistry would be required to be definitive (we have T cell markers only at the moment). Most cases of multifocal cutaneous lymphosarcoma in dogs are progressive, with the development of additional cutaneous lesions and metastasis to regional lymph nodes and internal organs. Lymphoma of the skin is rare in all species, but is more commonly seen in dogs and cats. The mean age in dogs and cats is 10 years. There is no breed predilection in cats, but English Cocker spaniels, Bulldogs, boxers, Scottish Terriers and golden retrievers are predisposed to cutaneous lymphoma. Most of the tumours are on the trunk, but lesions can appear anywhere on the body. Cutaneous lymphoma tends to be a progressive disease, beginning with the development of multicentric skin tumours, and ultimately involving the regional lymph nodes and viscera. Non-epitheliotropic lymphomas tend to be more aggressive and rapidly progressive. Treatments based on standard chemotherapy regimens used for other forms of lymphoma have been used. Although some treatments have extended survival times, most are aimed at palliation. Ref: Tumors in Domestic Animals Fifth Edition. Edited by Donald J. Meuten. 2017 John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

History: History of IMHA, currently on treatment. Now has a small ulcerated lesion on the left lip-Demodex???, but concerning the has a very large 4 cm firm left mandibular lymph node. History: Metastatic mass lesions throughout the chest and abdomen, enlarged mesenteric nodes, mass lesions along the pleura and surrounding the aorta. Slides examined: 3/3 lung mass 4/4 hepatic node Cytology description: Lung mass: The smears are markedly blood contaminated, low in cellularity, with poor cellular preservation. Occasional mature adipocytes and frequent clear vacuoles are scattered in the background. Few small clumps of largely ruptured cells are scattered in the smears. Non-degenerate neutrophils appear proportional to possibly mildly increased compared to the level of blood contamination in some areas. Infectious organisms are not readily identified. Hepatic node: The smears are moderately blood contaminated with mild cellularity and sub optimal cellular preservation. The background is pale with few clear vacuoles and occasional ruptured adipocytes. Non-degenerate neutrophils may be mildly increased compared to the level of blood contamination. Rare vacuolated macrophages are also noted. Out of the few lymphocytes that have exfoliated intermediate lymphocytes are expanded. These cells have a high N: C ratio, low to slightly expanded amount of basophilic cytoplasm, round to oval to indented nuclei (approximately the diameter of a neutrophil) with finely stippled chromatin pattern and indistinct nucleoli. Few small lymphocytes are also scattered individually in the sample. Infectious organisms are not readily identified. Few cytoplasmic fragments are noted in the background Interpretation: Lung mass: Non-diagnostic sample Hepatic node: Limited yield sample, possible mild neutrophilic inflammation, expanded intermediate lymphocyte population (see comments) Comment: Lung mass: Unfortunately the poor cellular yield and poor cellular preservation precludes cytological interpretation. Some lesions can be poorly exfoliative. In these cases biopsy for histopathology is often more diagnostically rewarding than re-aspiration. Hepatic node: Unfortunately the smears from the hepatic node are also poorly cellular which precludes definitive diagnosis. Out of the low numbers of lymphocytes present intermediate lymphocytes are expanded and predominate in some areas. Although predominance of intermediate lymphocytes raises some concern for lymphoma, given the sample is very low in cellularity, it may not be entirely representative of the mass and a reactive population cannot be excluded. Neutrophils also appear mildly increase so inflammation at this site or inflammation in the area drained by the node may be present. Re-aspiration of the node as well as all other enlarged internal and peripheral lymph nodes is advised. Alternatively consider biopsy and histopathology for more information. Thank you for the excellent history and submission.

History: Entire male bulldog with very large mandibular LN's - aspirated suspected lymphoma? Also has suspected retrobulbar or ocular neoplasia left eye Slides examined: (sites clarified with Christina, smears labelled at lab) 2/2- Suspected R submandibular LN 1/1- Suspect L submandibular LN Cytology description: Suspected R submandibular LN: The smears are well preserved and of adequate cellularity with moderate blood contamination. Foamy salivary epithelial cells seen in small clusters are present in moderate numbers. Fewer clusters of polygonal, possibly ductal epithelium are also seen. Non-degenerate, variably karyolytic, and pyknotic neutrophils are moderately increased compared to the level of blood contamination. Individually located vacuolated macrophages are observed in lower numbers along with very mildly increase in small and intermediate lymphocytes. The background contains occasional basophilic streaming material with windrowing of cells; consistent with viscous salivary fluid. No infectious agents are identified. Suspect L submandibular LN: The smear contains a small area of cellularity composed of moderate numbers of non-degenerate neutrophils and rare vacuolated macrophages on a moderately blood contaminated background. Salivary epithelial cells are not present in this smear Interpretation: Suspected R submandibular LN: Consistent with moderate neutrophilic rich sialadenitis Suspect L submandibular LN: Evidence of moderate neutrophilic rich inflammation Comment: The cytologic findings from the suspected R submandibular LN are consistent with aspiration of salivary gland. There is evidence of inflammation here, so it seems likely that the mass/enlargement is of salivary origin rather than lymph node. Sialadenitis in dogs is an uncommon disease and has been associated with trauma, systemic or localized infection, and immune-mediated diseases. The smear from the suspect L submandibular LN is low yield and does not have any exfoliated salivary epithelial cells but neutrophilic rich inflammation is also present at this site. If clinically warranted, re-aspiration can be considered to determine if the L submandibular enlargement also reflects an inflamed salivary gland. I'm not sure if the sialadenitis may be related to the ocular/ retrobulbar lesion. Infectious organisms were not noted though consider collecting samples for culture to further investigate concurrent sepsis. The cytological findings are not supportive of lymphoma. Thank you for the interesting history and sample.
